intro: Martha Goldstein plays the Ballade No. 3 in A♭ major, Op. 47, on an Érard piano built in 1851. The opening material builds to a climax in A♭ major, and on the way the music passes through a rocking, dance-like section and a stormy passage in C♯ minor.

sections.label: A · Two voices in A♭ major
B · Dance theme on repeated Cs
sections.mNote: Broken octaves introduce a melody with off-beat accents.

sections.label: C · Right-hand semiquaver runs, leggiero
sections.mNote: The new melody is carried in semiquavers marked leggiero.

sections.label: B′ · Dance theme in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Left-hand runs beneath full right-hand chords.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme in octaves, A♭ major
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns in A♭ major, enlarged.

sections.label: Coda · Semiquaver runs and four final chords
sections.mNote: The semiquaver figure returns before the four closing chords.

cues.title: Opening theme in A♭ major
cues.text: The piano opens in A♭ major, marked dolce. Short phrases alternate between registers of the keyboard. The theme returns near the end, doubled in octaves across the full range of the piano.
cues.evidence: Opening and final return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Mieczysław Tomaszewski describes the first theme at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nohant, summer 1841
cues.text: Chopin wrote the Third Ballade in the summer of 1841, under George Sand’s roof at Nohant. The F-minor Fantasy and the two Nocturnes, Op. 48 date from the same summer.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski dates the Ballade to summer 1841: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110. The associated works and Nohant setting are summarised from Norbert Müllemann’s Henle preface at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: Second theme over repeated Cs
cues.text: The right hand moves back and forth between Cs an octave apart, marked mezza voce (half voice). A new melody grows out of this figure, with its accents placed between the strong beats.
cues.evidence: Repeated C octaves and mezza voce: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Syncopated second theme: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mickiewicz’s Świtezianka
cues.text: In 1841 Schumann wrote that Chopin had told him certain poems of Mickiewicz suggested his ballades. Tradition links the Third Ballade with Mickiewicz’s Świtezianka, about a water nymph and a hunter who breaks his oath of faithfulness. Nothing Chopin said ties the poem to this piece.
cues.evidence: Schumann’s 1841 review of the Second Ballade, quoted in Dorota Zakrzewska, ‘Alienation and Powerlessness: Adam Mickiewicz’s Ballady and Chopin’s Ballades’, Polish Music Journal 2 (1999): https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol2/mickiewicz-and-chopin/ . The Third Ballade’s usual association with Świtezianka: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: Dedication to Pauline de Noailles
cues.text: The dedication names Pauline de Noailles, one of Chopin’s pupils. She turned eighteen in the year he wrote this Ballade, and died in 1844, three years later.
cues.evidence: Dedication: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110. Pauline de Noailles’s dates, 1823–1844, and pupil relationship: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: Third theme, leggiero semiquavers
cues.text: A third idea enters in right-hand semiquavers, marked leggiero, back in A♭ major. The semiquaver runs carry their own melody, which returns once more in the closing bars.
cues.evidence: Leggiero semiquaver theme and its A♭-major reprise: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Its brief final return is also described by Tomaszewski.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Development in C♯ minor
cues.text: The rocking idea returns on A♭ and then moves into C♯ minor, where the same piano key is written as G♯. The left hand plays chromatic runs beneath large chords in the right hand.
cues.evidence: The broken-octave theme’s transposition, C♯-minor development and left-hand chromatic runs: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: A♭ major returns, and the opening melody comes back in octaves, with fuller chords and support from the bass.
cues.evidence: A♭-major return of the opening theme in octaves: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in A♭ major
cues.text: The leggiero A♭ major runs return for a last flourish, followed by a right-hand arpeggio. Four chords end the Ballade. Of Chopin’s four ballades, this is the only one to finish in a major key.
cues.evidence: Closing leggiero runs, arpeggio, four chords and major-key ending: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repeated Cs lead to the second theme
transitions.from: A · Two voices in A♭ major
transitions.to: B · Dance theme on repeated Cs
transitions.how: The A♭ major opening section closes. The right hand then alternates between Cs in two octaves, marked mezza voce. These repeated notes lead into the second theme, which has off-beat accents against the regular six-quaver bar.
transitions.evidence: Repeated Cs and mezza voce: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Syncopated theme: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.

transitions.title: Right-hand runs in A♭ major
transitions.from: B · Dance theme on repeated Cs
transitions.how: The rocking theme leads to a new idea in A♭ major, played by the right hand in semiquavers marked leggiero. The short repeated-note figures are replaced by continuous runs above the left-hand accompaniment.

transitions.title: A♭ becomes G♯
transitions.to: B′ · Dance theme in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The broken-octave figure returns on A♭. A change of key signature turns that note into G♯, the dominant of C♯ minor. The second theme grows into large right-hand chords, and the left hand takes up rapid chromatic runs.
transitions.evidence: Transposed broken-octave figure and C♯-minor development: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: Return of the opening in A♭ major
transitions.from: B′ · Dance theme in C♯ minor
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme in octaves, A♭ major
transitions.how: The chromatic left-hand runs widen beyond the octave, and the dynamic rises from piano to forte. The key signature changes back to A♭ major, and the opening melody returns in octaves over a heavier bass.
transitions.evidence: Chromatic retransition, dynamic markings and A♭-major octave return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: Return of the leggiero runs
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme in octaves, A♭ major
transitions.to: Coda · Semiquaver runs and four final chords
transitions.how: The opening theme’s octave statement leads to the A♭ major leggiero runs. The right hand plays the third idea again, then an arpeggio, and joins the left hand for four closing chords.
transitions.evidence: Final return of the third theme and four-chord close: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
